content: Glycine, abbreviated as Gly or G, is an organic compound with the chemical formula NH₂CH₂COOH. It is the smallest of the 20 amino acids commonly found in proteins, as its side chain consists of only two hydrogen atoms. Glycine is encoded by the codons GGU, GGC, GGA, and GGG. It is a colorless, sweet-tasting crystalline solid and is unique among proteinogenic amino acids because it is not chiral. Due to its simple structure, glycine can integrate into both hydrophilic and hydrophobic environments. Production and Key Properties Glycine was first discovered in 1820 by Henri Braconnot, who obtained it by boiling gelatin with sulfuric acid. Industrially, glycine is produced by treating chloroacetic acid with ammonia, with an annual production of approximately 15 million kilograms. In the United States, glycine is manufactured by GEO Specialty Chemicals, Inc., and in Japan by Shoa Denko, using the Strecker amino acid synthesis method. In the U.S., there are two main producers of glycine, which acquired production facilities from Dow/Hampshire Chemical Corp. The manufacturing processes differ slightly: Chattem’s process (MCA process) is batch-based and results in a product with residual chloride but no sulfate, while GEO’s semi-batch process yields a product with residual sulfate but no chloride. At a pH of 7.8, glycine predominantly exists as the anionic amine H₂NCH₂CO₂⁻. At a pH of 3.5, it is mostly present as the cationic carboxylic acid H₃N⁺CH₂CO₂H. Biosynthesis Glycine is not an essential amino acid in the human diet because it can be synthesized in the body from serine, which itself is derived from 3-phosphoglycerate. This transformation is catalyzed by the enzyme serine hydroxymethyltransferase, which uses pyridoxal phosphate as a cofactor. In vertebrate livers, glycine synthesis is also catalyzed by glycine synthase (also known as the glycine cleavage enzyme). This reaction is reversible. Glycine is encoded by the codons GGU, GGC, GGA, and GGG. While most proteins incorporate only small amounts of glycine, collagen is an exception, containing approximately 35% glycine. Degradation Glycine is degraded through three main pathways. The predominant pathway in animals involves the glycine cleavage enzyme, which is also involved in glycine biosynthesis. This degradation pathway is essentially the reverse of the synthetic pathway. In the second pathway, glycine is degraded in two steps: first, it is converted back to serine via serine hydroxymethyltransferase, and then serine is converted to pyruvate by serine dehydratase. In the third pathway, glycine is converted to glyoxylate by D-amino acid oxidase, and glyoxylate is subsequently oxidized to oxalate by hepatic lactate dehydrogenase in an NAD⁺-dependent reaction. Physiological Function The primary role of glycine is as a precursor for protein synthesis. It also serves as a building block for numerous natural products. As a Biosynthetic Intermediate In higher eukaryotes, glycine is a precursor for δ-aminolevulinic acid, which is a key intermediate in the biosynthesis of porphyrins. Glycine also provides the central C₂N subunit for all purines. As a Neurotransmitter Glycine functions as an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system, particularly in the spinal cord, brainstem, and retina. When glycine receptors are activated, chloride ions enter the neuron through ionotropic receptors, leading to an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP). Strychnine is a potent antagonist of ionotropic glycine receptors, while bicuculline is a weaker one. Glycine also acts as a required co-agonist, along with glutamate, for NMDA receptors. Unlike its inhibitory role in the spinal cord, glycine facilitates excitatory activity at NMDA glutamatergic receptors. The LD₅₀ of glycine in rats (oral administration) is 7930 mg/kg, and death is typically caused by hyperexcitability. Commercial Uses In the United States, glycine is sold in two grades: United States Pharmacopeia (USP) grade and technical grade. Most glycine is manufactured as USP-grade material for diverse applications. Pharmaceutical-grade glycine is produced for specific applications, such as intravenous injections, where purity requirements often exceed the minimum standards of USP-grade glycine. Pharmaceutical-grade glycine is typically manufactured to proprietary specifications and is sold at a premium compared to USP-grade glycine. Technical-grade glycine, on the other hand, is sold at a discount and is used in applications such as metal complexing and finishing. Animal and Human Foods USP-grade glycine is used as an additive in pet food and animal feed. For humans, glycine is marketed as a sweetener or taste enhancer. It is also included in food supplements and protein drinks. Certain drug formulations incorporate glycine to improve gastric absorption of the active ingredient. Cosmetics and Miscellaneous Applications Glycine is used as a buffering agent in antacids, analgesics, antiperspirants, cosmetics, and toiletries. It is also employed in the production of rubber sponge products, fertilizers, and metal complexants. Chemical Feedstock Glycine serves as an intermediate in the synthesis of various chemical products. It is a key component in the production of the herbicide glyphosate (N-(phosphonomethyl)glycine), a non-selective systemic herbicide used to eliminate weeds, particularly perennials. Glyphosate was initially sold exclusively by Monsanto under the trade name Roundup but is no longer under patent. Presence in Space The detection of glycine in the interstellar medium has been a topic of debate. In 2008, a glycine-like molecule, aminoacetonitrile, was discovered in the Large Molecule Heimat, a giant gas cloud near the galactic center in the constellation Sagittarius, by the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy. In 2009, glycine sampled in 2004 from comet Wild 2 by NASA’s Stardust spacecraft was confirmed, marking the first discovery of extraterrestrial glycine. These findings support the panspermia hypothesis, which posits that the seeds of life are widespread throughout the universe.
